props.title: The Greatest Story Ever Told
props.initialSlug: Epic retelling of Jesus Christ's life and ministry

sections.content: The Greatest Story Ever Told stands as one of Hollywood's most ambitious biblical epics, with director George Stevens assembling an unprecedented all-star cast to tell the life of Jesus Christ. Unlike Cecil B. DeMille's more action-oriented The Ten Commandments (1956), Stevens aimed for a more contemplative, artistic approach. The film's massive $20 million budget (equivalent to over $170 million today) went into creating elaborate sets across multiple states, with Utah's landscapes standing in for the Holy Land. Max von Sydow's serene, internalized portrayal of Jesus marked a significant departure from previous Hollywood depictions, though the controversial casting of John Wayne as a centurion remains one of cinema's most discussed cameos.

sections.content: The 1960s marked the peak and eventual decline of the biblical epic genre. Barabbas (1961) with Anthony Quinn offered a unique perspective by following the man released instead of Jesus. The Bible: In the Beginning... (1966) attempted to tackle the Book of Genesis but marked the end of the big-budget biblical era. The genre's elaborate production values and all-star casts became financially unsustainable as audience tastes shifted toward contemporary stories. Modern biblical films like Noah (2014) and Exodus: Gods and Kings (2014) attempted to revive the genre with CGI spectacle, but none achieved the reverent grandeur of the classical era. SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Artistic Influence

Stevens' cinematographic choices in The Greatest Story Ever Told influenced religious filmmaking for decades. The director collaborated with cinematographer William C. Mellor and later Loyal Griggs (after Mellor's death during production) to create painterly compositions inspired by religious art, particularly Renaissance masters. This artistic approach influenced later films like Franco Zeffirelli's Jesus of Nazareth (1977) and Martin Scorsese's The Last Temptation of Christ (1988), though each brought their own distinct visual interpretation to the biblical narrative.
